runs.query: How does acme split its self-hosted CI tooling between runners and control planes?

answer.tldr:
Acme's self-hosted CI fleet splits into two halves. **Runner-side tools** execute work on hardware you already own, and that is where the throughput wins are: `acme/runner-pool` (24.6k stars, Go) leases ephemeral runners onto spare capacity, `acme/cache-warden` shares one build cache across branches, and `acme/toolchain-pin` keeps every job on the same compiler. **Control-plane services** decide and record rather than execute: `acme/build-journal` and `acme/release-train` own what shipped and when, while `acme/rollout-gate` holds a release until its named checks report green.

| Rank | Repo | Stars | Language |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | acme/runner-pool | 24.6k | Go |
| 2 | acme/build-journal | 18.2k | Rust |
| 3 | acme/artifact-store | 15.9k | Go |
| 4 | acme/pipeline-lint | 12.4k | TypeScript |
| 5 | acme/release-train | 11.1k | Python |

bullets.text: `acme/runner-pool` (24.6k) leads the runner-side tier; Go, updated within 2 days.
`acme/build-journal` and `acme/artifact-store` are the control-plane record keepers.
`acme/cache-warden` and `acme/env-broker` are what cut queue time on shared hardware.
`acme/pipeline-lint` is the only one that runs before a pipeline ever executes.
Two field guides corroborate the runner-vs-control-plane split.

runs.query: Which acme repos are starter templates rather than running services?

The acme repos that ship **something you copy** rather than something you run are indexes, stage libraries and scaffolds. `acme/pipeline-recipes` (9.6k) is the canonical index; `acme/stage-library` and `acme/repo-scaffold` are the busiest ready-to-fork sources.

| Rank | Repo | Stars | Type | URL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | acme/pipeline-recipes | 9.6k | index | git.example.com/acme/pipeline-recipes |
| 2 | acme/stage-library | 7.2k | library | git.example.com/acme/stage-library |
| 3 | acme/repo-scaffold | 5.4k | scaffold | git.example.com/acme/repo-scaffold |
| 4 | acme/runner-images | 4.9k | images | git.example.com/acme/runner-images |
| 5 | acme/pipeline-lint-hook | 3.1k | hook | git.example.com/acme/pipeline-lint-hook |

answer.tldr: **bearlike/Assistant** (a.k.a. Mewbo) is an AI assistant modelled as a conversation state machine with a hierarchical agent hypervisor. A single async `ToolUseLoop` binds an LLM via native tool-calling; sub-agents are admitted through `spawn_agent` and tracked by an `AgentHypervisor`. Interfaces span a CLI, a web console, a REST API, Home Assistant and an Android client, all sharing one core engine.

bullets.text: The core engine is one async `ToolUseLoop` bound to an LLM.
Sub-agents resolve to one of four terminal states via the hypervisor.
The DeepWiki entry summarizes the monorepo's layered architecture.

runs.query: Why is the rejected-plan color amber not red?

memory.content: github#search_repositories ranks best by stars then pushed-at; combine both for 'popular + active'.
github#list_commits confirms activity: filter to commits in the last 14 days to drop stale repos.
github#get_repository is the source of truth for license + primary language on a result card.
github#search_code is noisy for library discovery; prefer search_repositories then read code.
github#search_issues surfaces 'awesome-*' lists indirectly; scope with 'in:name awesome'.
github#get_file_contents on README.md yields the pitch line for a snippet.
github#get_latest_release dates tell you maintenance cadence better than stars alone.
github#list_pull_requests open-count is a cheap liveness signal for a repo.
huggingface#hub_repo_search spans models, datasets and spaces; set type to disambiguate.
huggingface#hub_repo_details downloads count is the Hub analog of GitHub stars.
huggingface#model_search by task is the fastest path to 'best model for X'.
huggingface#dataset_search modality filter avoids returning models by mistake.
huggingface#space_search finds live demos but rarely source; pair with a GitHub lookup.
huggingface#hf_doc_search is good for API usage, weak for repo discovery.
gitmcp#fetch_generic_documentation needs owner+repo already resolved; run the mapping first.
gitmcp#match_common_libs_owner_repo_mapping resolves a bare library name to owner/repo cheaply.
gitmcp#search_generic_code is scoped to one repo; do not use it for cross-repo discovery.
gitmcp#fetch_generic_url_content cleans doc pages well for citation snippets.
deepwiki#ask_question is the fastest architecture summary for a known repo.
deepwiki#read_wiki_structure lists topics; use it to target read_wiki_contents.
deepwiki#resolve_repo tolerates fuzzy names; run before ask_question on ambiguous input.
deepwiki#list_available_repos is small; not every repo has a generated wiki.
context7#resolve_library_id must run before any query_docs call.
context7#query_docs with a tight topic beats fetching the whole docs bundle.
context7#search_symbols is the right tool for 'does library X expose API Y'.
context7#list_versions matters when a question pins a specific release.
internet-search#searxng_web_search is the discovery entry point; read the top pages after.
internet-search#web_url_read is the cite-quality reader; always read before quoting.
internet-search#news_search is better than web_search for 'latest' or 'this week' queries.
internet-search#searxng_search_suggestions helps widen a thin query, not to answer it.
internet-search#image_search rarely helps repo discovery; skip it for code queries.
Cross-source: resolve a library via gitmcp mapping, then confirm stars via github#get_repository.
